name: Caudate nucleus, head
function: The enlarged anterior caudate forms a bulge along the lateral wall of the frontal horn, medial to the anterior limb of the internal capsule. It participates in associative, oculomotor and motivational corticostriatal loops; functional territories overlap rather than dividing cleanly at the head/body boundary.

afferent: Prefrontal, cingulate and other corticostriatal glutamatergic inputs
Nigrostriatal dopamine and intralaminar thalamic inputs
efferent: GABAergic projections to pallidal segments and substantia nigra pars reticulata
Outputs organized in direct/indirect and additional recurrent basal-ganglia networks

bloodSupply: Recurrent artery of Heubner/other ACA perforators and MCA lenticulostriate branches, with variable territories.

clinical.findings: Can produce abulia, executive/behavioral changes or language/attention deficits according to side and associated injury; a motor deficit often reflects adjacent capsule involvement.
Striatal degeneration, including caudate and putamen, contributes to motor, cognitive and psychiatric manifestations; caudate atrophy can enlarge the frontal horns.
clinical.note: Degenerative, not a focal vascular syndrome.

name: Caudate nucleus, body
function: The caudate body follows the lateral ventricle body, lateral to the thalamus; the stria terminalis and thalamostriate vein mark the caudate-thalamic groove. It is continuous with the head and tail and participates in topographically organized corticostriatal networks.

afferent: Corticostriatal, nigrostriatal and intralaminar thalamic inputs

bloodSupply: Predominantly MCA lenticulostriate branches, with variable posterior contributions.

clinical.findings: May cause cognitive/behavioral changes; motor or sensory deficits depend on neighboring capsule/thalamic involvement.
Can extend into the lateral ventricle and cause hydrocephalus or impaired consciousness; focal deficits depend on extent.

name: Caudate nucleus, tail
function: The tapering caudate tail curves posteriorly around the thalamus and forward along the roof of the temporal horn toward the amygdala. Temporal/visual association inputs contribute to caudate-tail networks; anatomical proximity to amygdala does not make it a continuous bridge to ventral striatum.
bloodSupply: Variable anterior choroidal and posterior cerebral contributions to posterior/temporal caudate territory.

clinical.findings: Isolated caudate-tail deficits are difficult to establish. Anterior choroidal stroke may also involve capsule/visual pathways, whose injury explains the major motor/sensory/visual signs.

name: Putamen
function: The putamen is the lateral component of the lentiform nucleus and a major sensorimotor striatal input region. It lies lateral to pallidum, separated from the insula by external capsule, claustrum and extreme capsule. Its motor, associative and limbic territories overlap within corticostriatal networks.

afferent: SNc dopaminergic and centromedian-parafascicular thalamic inputs
efferent: GABAergic projections to GPi/SNr and GPe in the classical direct/indirect pathways

bloodSupply: Mainly MCA lenticulostriate branches, with variable anterior choroidal/ACA contributions.

clinical.findings: May cause contralateral weakness/sensory loss through adjacent capsule injury, with gaze or consciousness changes when extensive.
Loss of nigrostriatal dopamine alters striatal and wider basal-ganglia activity; the primary degenerating population is in SNc.
clinical.note: Common DBS targets are STN or GPi; this record is not a treatment recommendation.

name: Globus pallidus, external segment
function: GPe is the lateral pallidal segment, between putamen and GPi, separated by medullary laminae. It provides inhibitory projections to STN and other basal-ganglia targets and receives substantial excitatory STN input. The indirect-pathway teaching model captures only part of its recurrent circuitry.

afferent: Glutamatergic STN input and recurrent pallidal connections
efferent: GABAergic projections to STN, GPi/SNr and striatal targets, varying by cell population

bloodSupply: MCA lenticulostriate and anterior choroidal supply, with variability.

clinical.findings: Focal or bilateral pallidal damage can accompany movement disorders, but dystonia is not predicted reliably by a simple GPe-STN firing-rate chain.
Carbon monoxide and other hypoxic/toxic exposures can involve both pallidal segments and wider brain networks; patterns vary.
clinical.note: Avoid treating all toxins as selective GPe lesions.

name: Globus pallidus, internal segment
function: GPi is the medial pallidal segment next to the internal capsule and is a major GABAergic basal-ganglia output nucleus alongside SNr. Pallidothalamic axons travel via ansa lenticularis/lenticular fasciculus into the thalamic fasciculus; outputs also reach brainstem targets. Firing patterns and network timing are as relevant as mean rate.

afferent: Direct striatal inhibitory and STN excitatory input
GPe and other modulatory/recurrent basal-ganglia inputs

bloodSupply: Anterior choroidal and lenticulostriate arteries, with overlapping variable territories.

clinical.findings: Pallidal injury can produce dystonia, parkinsonism or hyperkinetic syndromes depending on extent and network effects.
GPi is an established target in selected movement disorders. DBS changes network activity and is not simply equivalent to silencing GPi or proof of the classical rate model.
clinical.note: Therapeutic context; patient selection requires specialist assessment.

name: Ventral striatum
function: The ventral striatum includes nucleus accumbens and ventromedial caudate/putamen territories near the basal forebrain. It integrates cortical and limbic information with dopaminergic modulation in motivation, reinforcement learning and action selection. It overlaps the accumbens record rather than representing a separate encapsulated nucleus.

afferent: Hippocampal/subicular and amygdalar input; VTA dopamine
efferent: Ventral pallidum and other basal-ganglia targets
Hypothalamic/brainstem and recurrent motivational network pathways

bloodSupply: ACA/Heubner and MCA perforating branches with variable overlap; no single fixed watershed boundary is established here.

clinical.findings: Ventral-striatal networks are implicated in addiction, compulsive behavior and mood disorders; these diagnoses cannot be assigned to a small atlas coordinate.
May alter drive, reward-guided behavior or executive function; effects depend on wider basal-forebrain/frontal involvement.

name: Nucleus accumbens
function: Nucleus accumbens occupies the ventral junction of caudate and putamen and is part of ventral striatum. Core/shell subdivisions participate in overlapping reward, motivational and learning circuits. Detailed rodent infralimbic/prelimbic terminology should not be treated as a one-to-one human cortical map.

afferent: Medial/orbitofrontal cortical, amygdalar and hippocampal/subicular inputs
efferent: Ventral pallidum and other basal-ganglia motivational networks
Hypothalamic and midbrain connections, varying by subregion

bloodSupply: Variable ACA/Heubner and MCA basal perforator contributions; this schematic record is not an arterial boundary map.

clinical.findings: Human imaging and experimental work implicate accumbens-centered networks in reinforcement and incentive motivation; dopamine does not simply convert pleasure into craving.
Accumbens/ventral-capsule stimulation has been studied for refractory psychiatric disorders; indication, efficacy and approval differ by condition and jurisdiction.
clinical.note: Research/selected clinical context, not a general treatment claim.

name: Ventral pallidum
function: The ventral pallidum is a basal-forebrain pallidal region below the anterior commissure, continuous with ventral pallidal territories. It receives ventral-striatal input and participates in reward, motivation and action through thalamic, hypothalamic and midbrain connections. Findings about taste-reactivity hotspots largely derive from animal experiments.

afferent: Limbic, midbrain and other basal-ganglia inputs
efferent: MD and other thalamic targets linking to prefrontal cortex

bloodSupply: Variable basal perforating arteries from ACA/MCA and adjacent carotid-system branches; subregional territory is not independently mapped here.

clinical.findings: Injury involving this region may contribute to reduced motivation or behavioral change, but a unique human ventral-pallidal lesion syndrome is not established.
Animal manipulations support reward/hedonic functions; they do not establish that a focal human lesion abolishes all pleasure.
clinical.note: Species and experimental manipulation must be distinguished from clinical evidence.

name: Claustrum
function: The claustrum is a thin gray-matter sheet between external capsule medially and extreme capsule laterally, deep to insular cortex. It has extensive reciprocal cortical connections and is anatomically adjacent to, but not a standard component of, the motor basal-ganglia circuit. Its precise contribution to attention, integration and consciousness remains under investigation.

efferent: Reciprocal claustrocortical projections with regional organization

clinical.findings: Infarction, inflammatory injury or seizure-associated changes may involve claustrum with adjacent insula/capsules. There is no unique, validated claustrum-only consciousness syndrome.
Throat/visceral symptoms can occur in operculo-insular networks; they should not be attributed uniquely to claustrum.
